name: Pogs
blurb: Cardboard milk caps you stacked and hit with a slammer, a mid-1990s schoolyard craze
title: What Are Pogs? The 1990s Milk Cap Game and Why Schools Banned It
description: Pogs were collectible cardboard milk caps knocked over with a heavy slammer. Born in Hawaii, the game swept schools in the mid-1990s and was widely banned.
answer: Pogs were small, round cardboard discs, originally milk-bottle caps, used in a game where you stacked them face down and hit the stack with a heavier disc called a slammer, keeping the ones that flipped face up. The game came from Hawaii, was revived there in 1991 and became a worldwide craze that peaked in the mid-1990s. Many schools banned it as a form of gambling, and the fad was over by about 1997.

body: A pog is a flat cardboard circle a little bigger than a coin, printed on one or both sides; the commercial ones of the 1990s were thicker and glossier than the old dairy caps. A slammer is about the same width but heavier, usually plastic, rubber or metal.

ol: Each player puts the same number of pogs into one stack, face down.
Players take turns throwing the slammer onto the stack so the pogs scatter.
Any pog that lands face up goes to the player who threw.
The face-down ones are restacked for the next turn, until none are left; whoever has the most wins.

body: Players agreed beforehand whether they were playing "for keeps", meaning the winner kept the pogs, or just for fun. Rules varied from school to school.

body: Strictly, "POG" was a trademark and the generic name was "milk caps", but almost everyone called them Pogs. At the peak they were given away with Happy Meals and even with new bank accounts.

Because children kept the caps they won from each other, many school districts treated playing for keeps as gambling. Teachers also complained about classroom distraction and playground arguments over who had won what. Schools across North America banned the game, and it was also banned in parts of Australia and Sweden.

Like most toy fads, Pogs faded as fast as they arrived; by the late 1990s the companies behind them had moved on or closed. There have been occasional relaunch attempts since, but nothing close to the original craze. Today Pogs and slammers mostly turn up as second-hand lots and in collections, and the game itself needs nothing more than a stack of caps.

faq.a: Passion fruit, orange and guava, the flavors of a Hawaiian juice made by Haleakala Dairy whose bottle caps gave the game its name.

faq.q: Why were Pogs banned in schools?
faq.a: Mainly because playing for keeps looked like gambling, and because the game caused distraction and fights. Bans spread across North America in the mid-1990s.
Usually not much. They were printed by the million, so ordinary ones are common; only scarce or unusual sets in good condition interest collectors.
